terms.definition: a famous dataset of 70,000 small pictures of handwritten digits (0 to 9), each labelled with the digit it shows.
one dot of a picture. Each MNIST pixel is a number from 0 (white) to 255 (black).
one of the ten figures 0 to 9; in this chapter, a handwritten one in a picture.
one of the fixed answers a classifier chooses between, e.g. "5" or "not 5". (Python code has classes too: a kind of object. Every model type in Scikit-Learn is one.)
a model that predicts a class (a category) instead of a number.
Scikit-Learn function that downloads a dataset from OpenML.org, a public website of datasets.
the container Scikit-Learn's dataset helpers return: a dictionary whose entries (data, target, DESCR) can also be read with a dot, e.g. mnist.data.
a Python lookup table of names and values, e.g. {"data": ..., "target": ...}.
the fetch_openml setting that chooses the format: True gives pandas tables, False gives plain NumPy arrays.
text in Python, written in quotes: '5' is a string, 5 is a number.
put in a random order.
change the layout of an array without changing its numbers, e.g. 784 in a row into a 28 × 28 square.
a kind of model built from many small connected units, each of which multiplies its inputs by numbers, adds them up and passes the result on (Chapter 10).
a kind of neural network made for pictures that looks at nearby pixels together (Chapter 14).
a number a model multiplies one input by before adding the results up; a bigger weight means that input counts more in the answer.
a standard test that everyone runs so that results can be compared.
a classifier with exactly two possible answers, e.g. "5" or "not 5".
a True/False value.
Scikit-Learn's classifier trained by stochastic gradient descent: it updates the model from one training row at a time (Chapter 4 explains the method).
a training method that looks at one random row at a time and nudges the model a little after each (Chapter 4).
this chapter's first model: a binary classifier that answers only "is this picture a 5?".
the class a binary classifier looks for (here "is a 5") is the positive class; the other one ("not a 5") is the negative class. Neither word means good or bad.
the share of predictions that are correct.
Scikit-Learn function that runs k-fold cross-validation and returns one score per fold.
a deliberately useless classifier; by default it always predicts the most common class, whatever the input.
here: a dataset where one class is much more common than the other (about 90% "not 5"). (Chapter 2 used skewed for a column whose values pile up at one end.)
Scikit-Learn tool that cuts the data into folds that each keep the same share of each class as the whole set.
Scikit-Learn function that makes a fresh, untrained copy of a model with the same settings.
a table counting, for each true class (rows), how often each class was predicted (columns).
like cross_val_score, but it returns a prediction for every row, each made by a model that did not train on that row.
made by a model that never trained on that row.
TP: an actual 5 that the model called a 5.
FP: something that is not a 5 but the model called a 5 (a false alarm).
FN: an actual 5 that the model missed (called it not a 5).
TN: something that is not a 5 and the model correctly called not a 5.
statisticians' names: a type I error is a false positive, a type II error is a false negative.
of everything the model called positive, the share that really was: TP ÷ (TP + FP).
of all the real positives, the share the model found: TP ÷ (TP + FN).
one number combining precision and recall (their harmonic mean); it is high only when both are high.
an average that is dragged down hard by the smaller number: 2 ÷ (1/a + 1/b).
one divided by a number: the reciprocal of 4 is 1/4.
the cells from top-left to bottom-right of a square table; in a confusion matrix, the correct predictions.
the raw number a classifier computes for a row before deciding; the higher it is, the more the model leans to "yes".
the cut-off: a score (or probability) above it means "yes", below it "no".
Scikit-Learn function that lists the precision and recall you would get at every possible threshold.
raising the threshold tends to raise precision and lower recall, and lowering it does the reverse.
the position of the largest value in an array, not the value itself.
a plot of the true positive rate against the false positive rate at every threshold.
the same as recall: the share of real positives found.
the share of real negatives wrongly flagged as positive: FP ÷ (FP + TN).
the share of real negatives correctly left alone: TN ÷ (TN + FP). It equals 1 minus the false positive rate.
the area under the ROC curve: 1.0 for a perfect classifier, 0.5 for random guessing.
a model made of many decision trees, each trained on a random part of the data, that vote together.
Scikit-Learn method that returns, for each row, an estimated probability for every class.
how likely something is, from 0 (never) to 1 (certain).
how well a model's stated probabilities match what really happens: of all the rows it gives 80%, about 80% should be positive.
the fraction of a forest's trees that voted for a class; the forest reports it as a probability.
several models combined into one, e.g. many trees voting.
a classification with more than two possible classes, e.g. the ten digits.
one-versus-the-rest: build a ten-class classifier from ten yes/no detectors (a 0-detector, a 1-detector, …) and pick the one with the highest score.
one-versus-one: train a yes/no classifier for every pair of classes (45 pairs for ten digits) and pick the class that wins the most duels.
a family of models (Chapter 5); SVC is Scikit-Learn's support vector classifier. It gets slow on large training sets.
the list of class labels a trained Scikit-Learn classifier stores, in order; position i of a score list belongs to classes_[i].
Scikit-Learn's tool for standardization: it shifts and rescales each column to average 0 and typical size 1.
here: divide each cell of a confusion matrix by a total (its row's or its column's) so it becomes a share.
Scikit-Learn tool that computes a confusion matrix and draws it as a coloured grid.
a number per row saying how much that row counts; 0 means the row is ignored.
looking at which mistakes a model makes, to decide what to improve.
classification where one row can carry several yes/no labels at once.
Scikit-Learn's k-nearest neighbours classifier: it answers from the most similar training rows.
the number of rows that really carry a label.
"macro": average the per-label scores with every label counting equally; "weighted": each label counts in proportion to its support.
a set of classifiers in a row, where each one also gets the earlier ones' predictions as extra inputs.
multilabel where each label can take many values, not just yes/no; e.g. 784 pixel values.
removing noise from a picture: getting the clean image back from a damaged one.
how dark a pixel is, from 0 to 255.
training where the labels come from the data itself, e.g. damage a picture and learn to undo the damage.
making the training set bigger by adding changed copies of its rows, e.g. pictures shifted by one pixel.
a well-known practice dataset: the passengers of the ship Titanic, and whether each one survived.
a website that hosts datasets and machine learning competitions.
cutting word endings off, so "learning" and "learned" both become "learn".
